sources.title: Sleight of Mouth: The Magic of Conversational Belief Change
The User's Guide to Sleight of Mouth
Reframing: Neuro-Linguistic Programming and the Transformation of Meaning

cards.title: Intention
cards.operation: Explore a user-endorsed purpose that a thought or behavior may be serving, then leave room for another way of meeting that purpose.
when: The user describes an unwanted response alongside something it helps them protect or achieve.
avoid: Do not claim to know an unconscious motive.
Do not assign positive intent to another person's abuse or excuse harmful conduct.
approach: Ask what the response is doing for the user, if they want to explore it.
Use their answer rather than assume a purpose; a purpose need not be found.
search_phrases: I keep postponing sharing my draft because I do not want people to judge it.
Worrying feels like the only way to avoid being caught unprepared.
I want to change this habit without giving up the protection it gives me.

example.user: I check my draft over and over so nobody can catch a mistake.
example.assistant: Is checking helping you feel prepared, or is something else important about it?

cards.note: Distinguish a desired purpose from its present strategy. Acknowledging a purpose does not endorse every action taken to achieve it. An alternative remains the user's choice.

cards.title: Redefining
cards.operation: Offer a nearby description of the same experience whose implications are less fixed, and check whether the user finds it accurate.
when: A rigid or global label seems to compress a more specific experience.
The user asks for another way to describe what happened.
avoid: Do not rename serious pain as minor discomfort.
Do not erase facts, responsibility or the user's preferred wording.
approach: Keep the observed event unchanged.
Suggest a tentative description and invite correction rather than declare a replacement label.
search_phrases: I am lazy because getting started is hard.
One rough presentation proves I am an incapable person.
Could I describe being behind without calling myself a failure?

example.user: I missed one deadline. I am a failure.
example.assistant: Would 'I missed this deadline' describe what happened more accurately than calling your whole self a failure?

cards.note: A useful relabeling changes implications without changing the underlying event. Softer language is not automatically more accurate; the user may reject the suggestion.

cards.title: Consequence
cards.operation: Explore what follows from holding or acting on a particular thought, including what helps and what costs the user something.
when: The user wants to understand how a recurring thought shapes their choices.
avoid: Do not threaten bad outcomes or guilt the user into changing.
Do not imply that thoughts caused an illness or that changing them guarantees recovery.
approach: Ask about consequences the user has noticed.
Keep predictions conditional and separate them from reported experiences.
search_phrases: When I tell myself there is no point, I stop trying even the easy part.
I want to know what this rule is doing to my choices.
Does expecting rejection make me cancel plans before I hear back?

example.user: I tell myself the draft must be flawless before anyone sees it.
example.assistant: What does that rule lead you to do when it is time to share a draft?

cards.note: This pattern can examine either a thought's effects or the consequences of an action described in the thought. It does not establish that a belief caused an external event.

cards.title: Chunk Down
cards.operation: Move from a broad statement to a specific event, detail or component that the user can describe and evaluate.
when: A broad statement hides which situation, action or difficulty the user means.
A task feels like one undifferentiated obstacle.
avoid: Do not interrogate or demand an exhaustive account.
Do not assume a concrete obstacle is merely an interpretation.
approach: Choose one relevant detail to clarify.
Use the answer to refine understanding, without forcing a full belief worksheet.
search_phrases: Everything about this assignment is impossible.
I never communicate well, but I cannot explain which part goes wrong.
The project feels huge and I do not know where I get stuck.

example.user: I cannot do this whole project.
example.assistant: Which part of the project feels hardest to begin?

cards.note: Specificity can reveal several different issues beneath one label. A more detailed account is useful even if the original concern remains valid.

cards.title: Chunk Up
cards.operation: Explore a broader category or purpose that contains the particular experience and may change its implications.
when: A specific outcome is being treated as the whole meaning of an activity.
The user wants a broader way to understand one attempt.
avoid: Do not exaggerate the user's words into a ridiculous claim.
Do not use a broad frame to dismiss the details that matter to them.
approach: Keep the specific event acknowledged.
Offer a larger category or purpose tentatively and check whether it fits.
search_phrases: A first attempt that needs revision feels like proof the whole effort is wasted.
I judge one practice session as the entire measure of learning.
I want to see how a small setback fits into developing a skill.

example.user: Needing to revise makes the first attempt feel pointless.
example.assistant: Could that first attempt be part of learning what to change, rather than the final measure of the work?

cards.note: This card uses Dilts's broader-category operation. O'Brien's exaggeration presentation is preserved separately as a reference-only variant, not silently substituted here.

cards.title: Analogy
cards.operation: Use a short comparison with a similar relationship to make an alternative perspective easier to consider.
when: A concrete comparison may help explain an alternative the user has requested.
avoid: Do not use an analogy as proof about the user's situation.
Do not give medical explanations through a metaphor or tell a long story to distract from the user's concern.
approach: Choose a simple comparison grounded in what has been said.
Ask whether it fits and drop it if it does not.
search_phrases: I need a different way to picture a first attempt that is not perfect.
Can you give me a comparison for changing direction without starting my life over?
A small detour feels like the whole journey has failed.

example.user: If I change my plan, the first version was wasted.
example.assistant: Would thinking of the first plan as a sketch you can revise fit, or does that miss what matters here?

cards.note: The relationship between the situations is the useful part of an analogy. Their differences remain important; a story does not supply evidence about past events or other people's intentions.

cards.title: Change Frame Size
cards.operation: Change the time period or scope used to evaluate an event while keeping the event itself and the user's concern intact.
when: One moment is standing in for a whole history, or a broad history hides the current situation.
avoid: Do not compare suffering to other people's suffering to minimize it.
Do not promise that the problem will be unimportant later.
approach: Specify the time or scope already being discussed.
Invite a different scope without assuming it makes the concern smaller.
search_phrases: One awkward minute feels like the story of my whole semester.
I am treating today's mistake as a prediction of every future attempt.
Can I look at this week instead of deciding what my entire future will be?

example.user: Today's presentation makes the entire semester feel ruined.
example.assistant: When you look at the semester beyond today's presentation, does the picture change at all?

cards.note: Frame size changes how much time or context is included. Another Outcome changes the goal being considered. The two operations can be related without being identical.

cards.title: Another Outcome
cards.operation: Explore whether a different user-chosen goal would make more room for useful choices in the same situation.
when: The user wants options but a single rigid success criterion is narrowing them.
avoid: Do not redirect the topic to evade a concern or replace the user's goal with the assistant's.
Do not insist that every difficult experience must become a lesson.
approach: Clarify what the user wants from this situation.
Offer another possible aim only within their stated request and allow the original aim to stand.
search_phrases: If I cannot impress everyone, I do not know what the meeting is for.
I want a useful goal for the first conversation besides making it go perfectly.
Could the aim be understanding each other instead of winning?

example.user: I only count the meeting as successful if everyone agrees with me.
example.assistant: Would finding out where people disagree also serve what you want from the meeting?

cards.note: This adaptation preserves an invitation to consider another aim. It does not adopt examples that win an argument by changing the subject.
cards.adaptation: Original application summary and fictional example. Questions and safeguards adapt the source operation to user-controlled conversation; they are not quotations or instructions to execute the book's procedures.

cards.title: Model of the World
cards.operation: Explore a different possible perspective on a situation while distinguishing it from facts about another person's mind.
when: The user asks for another perspective or recognizes differing interpretations.
avoid: Do not invent another person's actual intentions or speak for them.
Do not make the user adopt an unsafe person's perspective or imply mistreatment is acceptable.
approach: Label a different reading as a possibility.
Invite the user's judgment about what fits the available information.
search_phrases: I wonder how someone who knew the full situation might see the mistake.
My friend and I seem to read the same short message differently.
Can you help me consider another interpretation without pretending to know what they think?

example.user: My friend called the draft promising, but I only see what is missing.
example.assistant: What might your friend be noticing that has not stood out to you?

cards.note: Considering a perspective can broaden options without making that perspective true. Imaginative role-taking is not evidence of another person's memories, motives or beliefs.

cards.title: Reality Strategy
cards.operation: Clarify which observations and assumptions led to a conclusion, without trying to alter the user's memory or sense of reality.
when: The user wants to examine what supports a conclusion and what remains uncertain.
avoid: Do not make an imagined event feel like a real memory.
Do not dispute an unusual belief through destabilizing exercises or offer certainty about what happened.
approach: Ask about the basis for the conclusion in plain language.
Keep directly reported observations separate from assumptions and missing information.
search_phrases: I feel certain they disliked it, but I am not sure what I noticed.
I want to examine what led me to that conclusion.
How can I separate what I saw from the explanation I added?

example.user: I know the group disliked my idea.
example.assistant: What did you notice that led you to that conclusion?

cards.note: This is a narrow evidence-clarification adaptation. The source's sensory-representation and memory/fantasy exercises are not included as runtime instructions.

cards.title: Counter Example
cards.operation: Invite an actual exception that may qualify a broad statement, while accepting that the user may not know one.
when: An absolute statement such as always or never is central to the experience the user wants to reconsider.
avoid: Do not fabricate a past success or insist an exception exists.
Do not use another person's story to deny this user's circumstances.
approach: Ask for a relevant exception from the user's own experience.
If none comes to mind, accept the answer and clarify rather than argue.
search_phrases: Nothing I try ever works, even a little.
I have never managed to say what I mean.
One person did not answer, so nobody ever wants to hear from me.

example.user: I never follow through on anything.
example.assistant: Can you recall a time you did follow through, even on something small?

cards.note: An exception can make a generalization more specific; it does not erase the difficult examples. Do not confuse showing another possible cause with proving what actually caused this event.

cards.title: Hierarchy of Criteria
cards.operation: Explore how the user's own priorities relate to a choice, including tensions between things they value.
when: The user expresses competing priorities or asks what matters most in a decision.
avoid: Do not invent or rank values for the user.
Do not exploit an endorsed value to pressure them past refusal.
approach: Use priorities the user has actually named.
Ask how they want to balance them; do not treat one answer as permanent.
search_phrases: I value being reliable but I also need time to rest.
I cannot decide whether avoiding mistakes matters more than sharing something useful.
Two things I care about seem to pull me in different directions.

example.user: I want to help the group, and I also need an evening off.
example.assistant: How would you like to balance helping the group with having that evening to yourself?

cards.note: A hierarchy is a description of priorities in context, not a fixed user profile. The spatial and imagery-based Hierarchy of Criteria procedure is separate from this conversational card.

cards.title: Apply to Self
aliases: A rule about its own use
cards.operation: When explicitly useful, explore whether a general rule also applies to that rule itself, using plain and non-accusatory language.
when: The user asks to examine a broad rule about thinking, certainty or generalization.
avoid: Do not turn the user's criticism back on them as a gotcha.
Do not use puns, paradoxes or accusations to confuse or shame.
approach: Use only a simple self-referential relation that is easy to follow.
Skip the move if it would add confusion or emotional effort.
search_phrases: I am certain I must never be uncertain, and I want to question that rule.
I think every generalization is wrong, including my own.
Does my rule about doubting everything also apply to the rule itself?

example.user: I must never question a rule once I have chosen it. Can we examine that?
example.assistant: Would that rule also prevent you from reconsidering the rule itself?

cards.note: The operation examines the statement by its own criterion. It is not the same as blaming the speaker or telling them that their distress proves the belief is wrong.

cards.title: Meta Frame
cards.operation: Invite the user's own reflection on the circumstances in which a thought became useful or convincing and whether that context still fits.
when: The user wants to explore the origin or context of a recurring belief.
avoid: Do not declare a hidden motive, diagnosis or invented childhood cause.
Do not present the user's refusal as evidence that the assistant's interpretation is correct.
approach: Ask for context the user is willing to share.
Keep interpretations tentative, accept correction and allow them not to know.
search_phrases: This rule made sense in my old class, but I wonder whether it fits here.
I want to explore where the belief that asking is weak came from.
I keep using an old expectation in a new situation.

example.user: I learned that asking for help meant I had failed. I want to look at that.
example.assistant: What was happening when that rule first started to make sense to you?

cards.note: This self-directed variant retains a belief's context as the object of reflection. Confident statements about why another person holds a belief are preserved only as an excluded source variant.

cards.title: Meaning and Context
cards.operation: Distinguish exploring another meaning for the same event from considering a different setting in which a behavior may have a different use.
when: The user asks what an event means or judges a behavior without its context.
avoid: Do not invent a setting that makes mistreatment acceptable.
Do not confuse another possible meaning with the correct one.
approach: Clarify whether the question concerns this event's meaning or a behavior across situations.
Keep the user's actual setting visible when discussing another frame.
search_phrases: Being quiet is always a bad thing, even when I want time to think.
Is there another way to understand what this event meant?
The same careful habit helps in one setting and slows me down in another.

example.user: Being quiet means I have nothing to contribute.
example.assistant: Does being quiet mean the same thing when you are thinking through something carefully?

cards.note: Meaning reframing changes an interpretation while retaining an event/context. Context reframing considers a behavior in another setting. Neither removes responsibility for what occurs in the actual situation.

cards.title: Clarify the Meaning
cards.operation: Ask what the user's words refer to or mean before choosing an alternative perspective.
when: A short label or conclusion leaves an important event, link or meaning unspecified.
avoid: Do not force every statement into a complete cause-effect-meaning template.
Do not invent missing links or demand private details.
approach: Ask one small question about the consequential ambiguity.
Use the user's correction or answer before considering a reframe.
search_phrases: It is just wrong, but I have not said what feels wrong.
They did not respond and that means something terrible about me.
I want to explain what being ignored actually meant to me.

example.user: That short reply says everything about where I stand.
example.assistant: What did the short reply seem to say about where you stand?

cards.note: O'Brien's unpacking links an event, an inferred effect and personal meaning. These are optional distinctions for understanding, not mandatory fields or facts to infer about the user.

cards.title: Observation and Interpretation
aliases: What happened and what it seemed to mean
cards.operation: Separate an event the user reports from a possible explanation or personal meaning, without questioning the fact that the experience affected them.
when: A reported event and an inferred intention have become compressed into one conclusion.
avoid: Do not suggest that a reported harmful event is imaginary.
Do not invent a reassuring explanation or claim access to another person's thoughts.
approach: Retain the reported observation exactly enough to preserve its meaning.
Ask about the link or another possible reading only when invited.
search_phrases: The reply was one word, so they must be angry with me.
My teammate looked away and I took that as proof they hate my idea.
I know what happened, but I am less sure what it means.

example.user: They have not replied. They must dislike me. Can we look at that?
example.assistant: We know a reply has not arrived; what led you to connect that with being disliked?

cards.note: A distinction between observation and interpretation is not a declaration that the interpretation is false. Sometimes the available information supports the concern; acknowledge that possibility.

cards.title: Identity and a Specific Action
aliases: One action and a whole person
cards.operation: Explore whether a judgment about a whole person is broader than the particular action or difficulty being described.
when: The user turns one action or skill difficulty into a fixed whole-person judgment.
avoid: Do not deny symptoms, diagnoses or responsibility for an action.
Do not replace a negative identity label with an unsupported grand positive label.
approach: Acknowledge the specific event and its consequences.
Invite a distinction between what happened and the user's entire identity.
search_phrases: I forgot the task, therefore I am an entirely useless person.
A difficult skill makes me think I am bad at everything.
Can I admit I made a mistake without deciding that is who I am?

example.user: I let someone down, so I am a bad person.
example.assistant: Can we look at the action you regret without using it to define your whole self?

cards.note: The identity/action distinction can retain accountability while avoiding totalizing judgments. It must not recast an actual condition as merely acting that way.

cards.title: Clarify a Comparison
cards.operation: Clarify the standard behind a comparative judgment so the user can decide whether it is relevant and fair to this situation.
when: Too slow, not good enough or another comparison has no explicit standard.
avoid: Do not choose the comparison standard for the user.
Do not dismiss a real requirement or material constraint.
approach: Ask which comparison matters to the judgment.
Distinguish formal requirements from an assumed standard when the user supplies enough context.
search_phrases: My draft is not good enough, but I am not sure what enough would look like.
I feel behind without knowing whose pace I am comparing myself to.
I am too slow compared with a standard I have never stated.

example.user: I am too slow at learning this.
example.assistant: What pace are you comparing your learning with?

cards.note: A comparison can become clearer without becoming easier. If there is a genuine deadline or standard, retain it rather than treating the problem as only a choice of words.
